statement:
In the plane, $2013$ red points and $2014$ blue points are marked so that no three of the marked points are collinear. One needs to draw $k$ lines, none of which passes through a marked point, dividing the plane into regions. The goal is that no region contain points of both colors.

Find the minimum value of $k$ for which the goal is attainable for every possible configuration of the $4027$ points.
solutions:
The answer is
\[
k=2013.
\]

For the lower bound, place $2013$ red points and $2013$ blue points alternately on a circle, and place the remaining blue point anywhere away from the circle, still keeping the no-three-collinear condition. The $4026$ arcs between consecutive marked points of the circle have endpoints of different colors. In a successful division, the endpoints of each such arc lie in different regions, so the arc must meet at least one of the drawn lines. A line meets the circle in at most two points and therefore meets at most two of these open arcs. Hence at least
\[
\frac{4026}{2}=2013
\]
lines are necessary.

We now show that $2013$ lines always suffice. We use two elementary separation facts.

First, any vertex of the convex hull can be separated from all other marked points by one line not passing through a marked point. Second, any two marked points $A,B$ of the same color can be separated together from all other marked points by two lines: take two lines parallel to $AB$, one on each side of $AB$, sufficiently close to $AB$. The open strip between them then contains exactly $A$ and $B$.

Let $P$ be the convex hull of all marked points.

\textbf{Case 1.} Suppose $P$ has a red vertex $A$. Separate $A$ from all other points by one line. Pair the remaining $2012$ red points into $1006$ pairs, and isolate every pair by two parallel lines as above. The number of lines used is
\[
1+2\cdot1006=2013.
\]
Every red point is separated from every blue point, so every resulting region is monochromatic.

\textbf{Case 2.} Suppose every vertex of $P$ is blue. Choose two consecutive vertices $A,B$ of $P$. A line parallel and sufficiently close to the supporting line $AB$ separates $A$ and $B$ together from all other points. Pair the remaining $2012$ blue points into $1006$ pairs and isolate each pair by two parallel lines. Again the total is
\[
1+2\cdot1006=2013.
\]
Thus the minimum is $2013$.

We prove the following more general statement:

\[
\text{Any }n\text{ red-and-blue points in general position can be separated by }\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor\text{ lines.}
\]

We use induction on $n$. The result is immediate for $n\le2$. Let $n\ge3$, and choose two marked points $A,B$ lying on a supporting line $\ell$ of the convex hull, so all other marked points lie strictly on one side of $\ell$.

Temporarily remove $A$ and $B$. By the induction hypothesis, the remaining $n-2$ points can be separated by
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{n-2}{2}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor-1
\]
lines. Put $A$ and $B$ back. There are three cases.

\textbf{Case 1.} The points $A$ and $B$ have the same color. Draw one line parallel to $\ell$, sufficiently close to it, separating $A,B$ from all other points. The separation is complete.

\textbf{Case 2.} The points $A$ and $B$ have different colors and are already separated by one of the previously drawn lines. Draw the same kind of line parallel to $\ell$, separating the pair $\{A,B\}$ from all other points. The old line separates $A$ from $B$, so the final regions remain monochromatic.

\textbf{Case 3.} The points $A$ and $B$ have different colors and lie in the same old region $R$. By the induction hypothesis, the old marked points in $R$ all have one color. Hence one of $A,B$ is the only point of its color in $R$; suppose it is $A$. Since $A$ is a convex-hull vertex, one can draw a line separating $A$ from every other marked point. This completes the separation.

In every case only one additional line is used, proving the induction. For $n=4027$ this gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{4027}{2}\right\rfloor=2013.
\]
Together with the lower bound from Solution 1, the answer is $2013$.
